title: Crêpes Suzette
subtitle: Thin crêpes in orange butter sauce, flambéed with Grand Marnier
excerpt: Thin crêpes cooked in an orange and butter sauce and flambéed with Grand Marnier at the table. One of the great French theatrical desserts, despite the entire recipe taking 30 minutes.
sourceNotes: The origin of crêpes Suzette is disputed. The most popular story attributes the dish to Henri Charpentier, who claimed to have accidentally created it in 1895 at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo while preparing dessert for the Prince of Wales and his companion Suzette. Escoffier also takes partial credit. Whatever the truth, the dish was standardised at the Café de Paris and Ritz Hotel in the early 20th century. Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), gives an early version. The alcohol flambage was a later addition to the recipe.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The crêpes can be made a day ahead and stacked with baking paper between each one. The Suzette butter can also be made a day ahead. Warm everything together in the pan just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of pouring a spirit into a hot pan and igniting it briefly. The flame burns off the raw alcohol, leaving only the flavour of the spirit. For crêpes Suzette, Grand Marnier or Cointreau is the traditional spirit. Stand back when igniting and have a lid ready in case the flame needs to be extinguished.

content.text: Crêpes Suzette has a reputation for complexity that it does not deserve. The crêpe batter rests for 30 minutes, then the crêpes are made, thin, almost translucent pancakes. The Suzette sauce is orange juice, orange zest, sugar, and butter, cooked together in a wide pan. The crêpes are folded in quarters and warmed in the sauce. The
at the end, Grand Marnier poured in and ignited, is the theatrical flourish rather than a technical challenge.
Whisk the flour with the eggs and a pinch of salt. Gradually whisk in the milk until a smooth, thin batter forms. Add the melted butter. Rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.

Heat the crêpe pan over medium-high heat and brush lightly with butter. Pour in a small ladleful of batter (about 3 tbsp) and immediately tilt the pan to spread it into a thin, even circle. Cook for 60 to 90 seconds until the edges are dry and the underside is golden. Flip and cook for 30 seconds more. Stack the cooked crêpes on a plate, they do not stick to each other.
Make the Suzette sauce and flambé
In a wide frying pan, melt the 60 g butter with the sugar over medium heat. Add the orange zest, orange juice, and lemon juice. Cook for 2 minutes until the sauce is slightly syrupy and bubbling.
Fold each crêpe in half, then in half again to make a quarter-circle. Place in the bubbling sauce, turning to coat. Arrange 3 to 4 crêpes overlapping in the pan.

Pour the Grand Marnier over the crêpes. If using a gas flame, tilt the pan slightly, the alcohol may ignite naturally. Otherwise, use a long match or long lighter. Stand back and allow the flames to die out naturally (10 to 15 seconds). Serve immediately, spooning the pan sauce over the crêpes.

items.symptom: The crêpes are tearing when flipped
items.cause: The batter was not rested, or the pan was not hot enough.
items.fix: A 30-minute rest allows the gluten in the flour to relax, making a more pliable crêpe. The pan must be properly hot before the batter goes in. A properly cooked crêpe releases cleanly from the pan when ready to flip.

items.symptom: The crêpes are thick and doughy
items.fix: Add more milk, a tablespoon at a time, until the batter pours easily and spreads thinly when tilted. Crêpe batter should be as thin as single cream.

items.cause: The pan was not warm enough, or the Grand Marnier was very cold.
items.fix: The pan must be hot when the alcohol is added. Warm the spirit gently first if it is very cold. A long lighter or long match is safer than a short one.

content.text: Whatever the precise origin story, crêpes Suzette was made famous at the grandest restaurants of the Belle Époque and became one of the defining tableside preparations of the early 20th century. The dish was made by the maître d'hôtel in a silver pan at the table, the flambée was as much theatre as cooking. As formal service declined, the dish retreated to the kitchen but retained its glamour. Today it is still the first French dessert that many people outside France can name, which speaks to the lasting power of a recipe designed as much to impress as to nourish.
